title: The History of Capcom | From Street Fighter To Resident Evil And Monster Hunter | Gaming History
description: The history of Capcom: Osaka arcade roots, Street Fighter and Mega Man in 1987, Resident Evil in 1996, Monster Hunter World and the recent remakes.
joke: Capcom has made so many hit series that even its lawyers have their own game.

sections.heading: The company behind the hits
sections.script: Welcome back to the channel. Today we are telling the history of Capcom, the Japanese company behind Street Fighter, Mega Man, Resident Evil, Devil May Cry, Monster Hunter and Ace Attorney. Few companies have created so many series that people still play and talk about decades later. Capcom started in Osaka in the late nineteen seventies, built its name in the arcades, found global fame on the PlayStation, and then reinvented itself with remakes and big new releases in the twenty tens and twenties. We will go through the early years, the arcade golden age, the survival horror breakthrough, the new franchises of the two thousands, the Monster Hunter boom, and the recent comeback. All dates come from Wikipedia and Capcom's own company history pages. Let us begin.

sections.heading: Osaka, nineteen seventy nine
sections.script: Capcom's roots go back to nineteen seventy nine, when a company called I.R.M. Corporation was founded by Kenzo Tsujimoto. The company made and sold arcade machines. In June nineteen eighty three, Capcom Co., Ltd. was established to take over the sales side of the business, and Capcom's own history page also dates the company's establishment in Osaka to nineteen eighty three. In its first years, Capcom made games for arcades and sold them around the world, and the company grew steadily as the arcade business boomed in Japan. Those early arcade releases gave the company the experience and the money to start building its own big franchises, and the following decade would be the one that changed everything.

sections.heading: Mega Man and Street Fighter
sections.script: Nineteen eighty seven was a huge year for Capcom, because two of its most famous series began. Street Fighter appeared in the arcades, and Mega Man arrived for home consoles. Mega Man starred a little blue robot who copied the powers of the bosses he defeated, and it became a symbol of tough, clever action platformers. Street Fighter was a one on one fighting game with special moves that players had to learn. Both would grow into long running series, and together they planted the seeds of the company's future. Capcom had found a style of game it did extremely well, which was tight controls, bold characters and difficulty that rewarded practice. That style would carry the company through the next decades.

sections.heading: Street Fighter II changes arcades
sections.script: In nineteen ninety one, Capcom released Street Fighter II, and the arcade world was never the same. Players chose from a roster of fighters with very different moves, such as Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li and Guile, and they challenged each other face to face. Wikipedia lists it as Capcom's highest grossing title, thanks largely to its arcade success. Crowds gathered around cabinets, and the game helped start the whole competitive fighting game scene. It also moved to home consoles, and Capcom's annual report records a Super NES release in nineteen ninety two. Street Fighter II proved that a Capcom game could become a worldwide cultural event, and it remains one of the most influential games in the history of the medium.

sections.heading: Resident Evil and survival horror
sections.script: In March nineteen ninety six, Capcom released Resident Evil on the PlayStation. Capcom's own history notes that it set sales records and helped establish survival horror as a genre. Players explored a spooky mansion with limited ammunition, fixed camera angles and tense puzzles, and the atmosphere was unlike most action games of the time. The series grew quickly, with sequels, spin offs, films and countless fans. In two thousand five, Resident Evil four arrived on the GameCube and received almost universal acclaim, with a new over the shoulder view that influenced many shooters afterwards. By two thousand twenty three, Capcom's annual report said the series had passed one hundred million units sold, which shows how big a hit that first mansion had become.

sections.heading: New series in the two thousands
sections.script: After Resident Evil, Capcom kept inventing. In two thousand one the company launched Devil May Cry, a stylish action game about a demon hunter named Dante, and the first Ace Attorney game, where you play a defence lawyer solving cases in a courtroom. In two thousand four came Monster Hunter, and in two thousand six came Dead Rising, a zombie game set in a shopping mall. Each of these became a series of its own, and each one showed Capcom's willingness to try a new idea instead of repeating old hits. A company known for fighters and horror now had stylish action, courtroom drama and co operative hunting in its catalogue, and that variety became one of its greatest strengths. It also meant that fans could find a Capcom game to suit almost any taste, from quick reflex action to slow, careful investigation.

sections.heading: Struggles and a new focus
sections.script: Not every year was easy. Street Fighter IV arrived in two thousand eight and brought fighting games back into the spotlight, but later years had setbacks. According to Wikipedia, Street Fighter V missed its sales target of two million in March two thousand sixteen. Around that time Capcom decided to refocus its approach. Resident Evil seven: Biohazard, released in two thousand seventeen, was the first game made under that new direction. It returned to the series' roots with a tense, first person horror experience in a single house, and it was a big success. The lesson was clear, which was to concentrate on the company's strongest franchises, improve the technology behind them, and make fewer but better games.

sections.heading: Monster Hunter goes worldwide
sections.script: In two thousand eighteen, Capcom released Monster Hunter: World, a game designed to bring the series to a much wider audience. Instead of big hunts for a small group of fans, it offered a seamless world, better controls and easier teamwork. Capcom's annual report for that year said it had passed nineteen million copies, the first title in Capcom's history to reach that mark. Wikipedia lists it as Capcom's best selling game. Monster Hunter Rise followed, and in February two thousand twenty five, Monster Hunter Wilds arrived. The series shows how patient work can pay off, because a franchise that began in two thousand four became one of Capcom's biggest successes more than a decade later.

sections.heading: The remake era
sections.script: Capcom's recent success also comes from looking back. In January two thousand nineteen it released Resident Evil two, rebuilt from the ground up with modern graphics, and in March two thousand twenty three it released a new version of Resident Evil four. Both were widely praised and sold millions of copies. Instead of copying the originals exactly, the remakes changed controls, pacing and presentation to feel fresh for new players while keeping the spirit that fans loved. Capcom's own sales tables show Resident Evil two at over twenty million copies and the new Resident Evil four at over seventeen million. Together, these releases brought lapsed fans back and attracted a younger generation, and they proved that a classic idea can still feel new when it is rebuilt with care and modern technology.

sections.heading: Your favourite Capcom series
sections.script: That was the history of Capcom, from an Osaka arcade company in the late seventies, through Mega Man and Street Fighter in nineteen eighty seven, Street Fighter II in nineteen ninety one and Resident Evil in nineteen ninety six, to Monster Hunter and the remakes of today. The company has survived hard years by trusting its best ideas and reinventing them for each generation. Even a short list shows how much variety is there, with robots, fighters, zombies, demon hunters, lawyers and giant monsters. So tell us, which Capcom series is your favourite, and which old game would you love to see remade next? Let us know in the comments below.
